##Part A : Creating Matrices

```{r}
m1<- matrix (1:9, nrow=3, ncol=3)
m1
```

```{r}
m2<- matrix (1:9, nrow=3, ncol=3, byrow=TRUE)
m2
```

```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
scores
```

#Questions
1. By default, R fills a matrix column by column (top to bottom). Adding byrow = TRUE changes this so R fills the matrix row by row (left to right).

2. R automatically restarts the sequence from the beginning to fill the missing 9th slot. That is why the value in position [3, 3] is 1. Also, R displays a warning because 8 is not an exact divisor of 9. This warns you that the vector length does not cleanly fit the matrix dimensions.

```{r}
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
```

##Part B — Subsetting Matrices

```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
scores[1, 2]
scores[1, ]
scores[, "Ben"]
scores[scores >= 90]
```

#Questions

3. Running class() on scores[1, ] or scores[, "Ben"] returns "numeric". R downgrades a single row or column from a 2D matrix to a 1D vector. R automatically drops unnecessary dimensions to save memory and simplify computation. Since a single row or column only has one dimension of elements, R simplifies it to a standard vector (unless you explicitly prevent it by using drop = FALSE).

4. The matching elements (e.g., values 92, 95, 90) do not necessarily form a full row or column. Because a matrix requires a strict grid shape (equal numbers of elements in every row and column), R cannot keep a 2D structure for arbitrary selections. Evaluated conditions like scores >= 90 test the entire matrix as a flat sequence of values. It returns only the matching elements as a simple 1D vector.

##Part B: Matrix Properties and Operations

```{r}
dim(scores)
nrow(scores)
ncol(scores)

scores_t <- t(scores)
scores_t
dim(scores)
dim(scores_t)

a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
b <- matrix(5:8, nrow = 2)

a + b

a * b

a %*% b
```

5. R multiplies numbers in matching positions directly together (position [1,1] times position [1,1], position [1,2] times position [1,2], and so on). R uses linear algebra rules. It calculates each entry by taking the dot product of a row from matrix a and a column from matrix b (multiplying elements across the row by elements down the column and adding them together).

6. Transposing a matrix swaps the rows and columns. The row names of scores ("Quiz1", "Quiz2") describe what each row represents. When you transpose the matrix, those rows become columns, so the original row names must become the new column names (and vice versa) so that the labels still correctly match their data.

##Part D: cbind() and rbind()

```{r}
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
scores_v2

scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3
```

#Questions

7. When you try to append 3 values to a matrix with only 2 rows using cbind(), R uses its recycling rule to fill the existing 2 rows (taking 85 and 91) and ignores the excess value (100), while throwing a warning message. cbind() and rbind() require matching dimensions because a matrix must maintain a perfect 2D grid shape (a rectangle). Every column in a matrix must have the exact same number of rows, and every row must have the exact same number of columns. Passing mismatched lengths breaks this geometric structure.

```{r}
cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))
```

8. You would use rbind() when you are adding new observations or records over time, rather than adding new variables or subjects.

##Part E — Arrays: Creating and Subsetting

```{r}
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
arr

arr[1, 2, 2]

arr[ , , 1]


dim(arr)
```

#Questions

9. The dim(arr) output is 2 3 2, where each number represents: 2 Rows, 3 Columns, and 2 Layers.

10. Tracking monthly sales data across multiple store locations and product categories over several years. Rows: Product categories (e.g., Electronics, Clothing). Columns: Store locations (e.g., Store A, Store B, Store C). 3rd Dimension (Layers): Time in years (e.g., 2024, 2025, 2026). A single 2D matrix is not enough because it can only track two factors at once (e.g., products by store). Adding a third factor, like year, requires a stacked layer for each period to keep the data organized without merging or repeating information.

##Part F — Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r}
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students

rowMeans(all_students)
```

#Questions

11. rbind() was used because class_a and class_b represent new students (rows) being added to the dataset, while keeping the same evaluation metrics (columns). The clue in the data was that both matrices share identical column names ("Midterm" and "Final"), but have distinct row names ("S1", "S2" vs. "S3", "S4"). When matrices share the same columns, you stack them vertically using rbind().

12. Use rbind() to stack all 5 matrices together in a single step (e.g., passing all 5 matrix objects into rbind()).To check if the result is correct using dim(), check that the column count remains 2 (since all classes share the same 2 exam columns), while the row count equals the total sum of all students across all 5 classes.

##Conclusion

A matrix is a two-dimensional grid of data made of rows and columns, whereas an array extends this concept into three or more dimensions by stacking multiple matrices into layers. Functions like cbind() and rbind() are useful when merging real-world datasets over time, such as combining monthly customer survey results (rbind()) or adding new calculated test scores to existing student records (cbind()).
